title: Composite, etching & bonding
blurb: How tooth-coloured composite sticks to teeth: shade, etch, bond, cure in increments, and using the curing light safely.
question: The dentist is about to restore a chipped upper central incisor with composite. You have the rubber dam ready, the etchant, the bonding agent and the curing light. In what order should things happen, and what would you do if saliva touched the tooth just after it had been etched and rinsed?

teach.body: Composite is a tooth-coloured filling material made of a resin matrix packed with fine glass or silica filler particles, joined by a coupling agent. It also contains a light-activated initiator, so it stays soft until it is exposed to high-intensity blue light from the curing light, then sets in seconds. It comes in many shades and types, from runny flowable composite to stiffer packable and bulk-fill materials. Composite does not stick to teeth by itself: it relies on etching and bonding.

Etchant (37% phosphoric acid gel, usually coloured blue so you can see it) dissolves a little mineral from the enamel surface and leaves it microscopically rough. Rinsing washes away the acid and dissolved mineral; dried enamel then looks frosty white. The bonding agent (adhesive) flows into the tiny pores and is light-cured, forming resin tags that lock into the tooth. The composite then bonds to that layer. Some modern systems combine steps (self-etch or universal adhesives), so always follow the system the dentist uses.

teach.caption: Etchant is usually coloured blue so you can see where it has been placed. Single-use applicator brushes go in the waste after each patient.

teach.body: Choose the shade at the very start, with the tooth clean and moist, in natural daylight where possible rather than under the bright operating light. Teeth dry out under rubber dam or cotton wool rolls and quickly look lighter and whiter. A shade picked from a dried tooth will look too light once the tooth rehydrates. If the shade must be judged later, let the tooth rehydrate first. Keep dispensed composite covered and away from the operating light, which can start to set it.

teach.caption: After curing, each layer has a slightly sticky surface. This oxygen-inhibited layer is normal and helps the next increment bond. Bulk-fill composites are designed for thicker layers: follow the product's instructions.

items: Keep the field dry with rubber dam where possible, plus good aspiration.
If saliva touches the tooth after etching, tell the dentist straight away.
The usual fix is to rinse, dry and re-etch as the bonding system directs, then carry on.
Never just carry on bonding over contamination: the bond will be weak and may fail.

items: Composite = resin + filler, set by blue light; it bonds micromechanically via etch and bond.
Etch with 37% phosphoric acid gel, rinse, dry: enamel looks frosty.
Saliva contamination after etching: tell the dentist, rinse, dry and re-etch.
Place in increments of about 2 mm to cure fully and limit shrinkage stress.
Shade before isolation in natural light; orange shield to protect eyes from the curing light.

summary: You can now explain what composite is and how it bonds to enamel, set out the placement sequence from shade selection to polishing, recognise the etchant syringe, bonding bottle, composite instrument and curing light, deal with contamination after etching, and protect yourself and the patient from etchant, resins and curing light.

A.q: Saliva contaminates the tooth after it has been etched and rinsed, but before bonding. What is the best action?
options: Carry on, as saliva is harmless here
Dry it with cotton wool and bond
Rinse, dry and re-etch per protocol
Increase the curing time to compensate
A.why: Saliva coats the etched surface and blocks the bond, so the area is rinsed, dried and re-etched as the system directs. Tell the dentist straight away.

whyNot.0: Saliva contamination weakens the bond and can cause the restoration to fail.
whyNot.1: Drying doesn't remove the saliva film that has coated the etched surface.
whyNot.3: Longer curing can't fix a contaminated bonding surface.

A.q: What is the usual etchant used before placing composite?
options: 10% polyacrylic acid
37% phosphoric acid gel
2% chlorhexidine gluconate
Sodium hypochlorite solution
A.why: Phosphoric acid gel at about 37% is the standard etchant for enamel before bonding.

whyNot.0: Polyacrylic acid is used as a mild conditioner before glass ionomer.
whyNot.2: Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic, not an etchant.
whyNot.3: Sodium hypochlorite is a root canal irrigant.

A.q: After a composite increment is light-cured, its surface is slightly sticky. What does this mean?
options: The composite was overheated while curing
The etchant was left on too long
The curing light has failed
Oxygen has inhibited the surface set
A.why: Oxygen stops the very surface from curing fully, leaving a thin sticky layer. It is normal and helps the next increment bond.

whyNot.0: Overheating doesn't cause a tacky surface.
whyNot.1: Etching time affects the enamel, not the surface of cured composite.
whyNot.2: A sticky surface layer appears even with a working light; it isn't a sign of failure on its own.

B.q: When should the shade for an anterior composite be selected?
options: Before the tooth is isolated
After rubber dam has been placed
After the tooth has been etched
Once the cavity has been prepared
B.why: Teeth dry out and look lighter once isolated, so the shade is chosen first, on a clean, moist tooth.

whyNot.1: Under rubber dam the tooth dehydrates and looks lighter than it really is.
whyNot.2: Etched enamel looks frosty white, which gives a false shade.
whyNot.3: By then the tooth may have dried out and parts of it have been removed.

B.q: Why is posterior composite usually built up in layers of about 2 mm?
options: To increase its fluoride release
To cure fully and limit shrinkage
To avoid using a bonding agent
To make finishing unnecessary
B.why: Thin layers let the light cure each one fully and reduce polymerisation shrinkage stress at the margins.

whyNot.0: Composite releases little or no fluoride, however it is placed.
whyNot.2: Bonding agent is still needed; increments don't replace it.
whyNot.3: Layered restorations still need finishing and polishing.

B.q: How should the dental nurse protect their eyes while the curing light is in use?
options: Look away from the light and close their eyes
Wear clear safety glasses only
Use an orange filter shield or glasses
Dim the operating light before curing
B.why: Orange filters block the intense blue light that can damage the retina.

whyNot.0: Looking away or closing your eyes isn't reliable protection and stops you assisting safely.
whyNot.1: Clear glasses protect against splashes but don't filter blue light.
whyNot.3: The operating light has nothing to do with protection from the curing light.

C.q: How does composite bond to enamel?
options: Through a chemical bond with calcium
By being packed into cavity undercuts
Through the fluoride that it releases
By resin tags locking into etched enamel
C.why: Etching roughens the enamel and the bonding resin flows into the pores, forming tags that lock in micromechanically.

whyNot.0: A chemical bond with calcium in the tooth describes glass ionomer.
whyNot.1: Undercuts are how amalgam is retained, as it doesn't bond.
whyNot.2: Composite releases little or no fluoride, and fluoride isn't how it bonds.

C.q: The dentist asks you to keep the dispensed composite ready on the bracket table. What should you do?
options: Leave it under the operating light
Warm it under the curing light so it flows
Cover it and keep it out of bright light
Mix it with bonding agent to soften it
C.why: Light-cured composite starts to set when exposed to light, including the operating light, so keep it covered.

whyNot.0: The operating light can start curing composite before it is placed.
whyNot.1: The curing light would set it before it reaches the tooth.
whyNot.3: Mixing it with bonding agent would change its properties and isn't how it is used.

C.q: A composite looks lighter than the neighbouring teeth just after a long appointment under rubber dam. What is the best action?
options: Replace the restoration straight away
Re-etch the enamel on adjacent teeth
Polish it until the shade looks darker
Let the teeth rehydrate, then reassess
C.why: Dehydrated teeth look lighter, so the shade should be judged again once the teeth have rehydrated.

whyNot.0: The mismatch may disappear once the teeth rehydrate, so replacing it now could be unnecessary.
whyNot.1: Etching healthy enamel won't change its shade and damages its surface.
whyNot.2: Polishing smooths the surface; it won't fix a false shade caused by drying.

reteach.title: Think of it like painting a smooth wall
reteach.question: Paint peels off a smooth, shiny wall unless you prepare it. How is bonding composite the same?

blocks.body: A decorator sands a shiny wall so paint has something to grip, cleans off the dust, applies a primer that soaks into the surface, then paints in thin coats that each dry properly. Composite is the same: etch roughens the enamel (sanding), rinsing removes the acid and debris (cleaning), bonding agent flows into the pores (primer), and composite goes on in thin layers, each cured (thin coats). If the wall gets wet or greasy after sanding, you clean and prepare it again. If saliva touches etched enamel, you rinse, dry and re-etch.

blocks.text: Pick the paint colour before you start sanding: choose the shade before the tooth is isolated and dries out.

explain.body: Use the shade guide on a clean, moist tooth, in natural light, before rubber dam goes on. Dry teeth look lighter. You may be asked to hold the shade tab next to the tooth.

test.q: Why is the shade NOT chosen after rubber dam has been in place for some time?
options: Rubber dam stains the enamel
The shade guide can't be disinfected
Dried teeth look lighter than normal
The curing light changes the shade
test.why: Isolated teeth dehydrate and look lighter, so a shade taken then would be too light.

whyNot.1: Shade guides are cleaned and disinfected between patients as normal.
whyNot.3: The curing light sets the composite but doesn't change the tooth's shade.

explain.body: 37% phosphoric acid gel roughens enamel; rinse thoroughly and dry until enamel looks frosty. Bonding agent is applied, thinned with air and cured, forming resin tags. Saliva contamination after etching means rinse, dry and re-etch.

items.label: Etchant
items.sub: Keep off soft tissue and eyes

test.q: What does correctly etched and dried enamel look like?
options: Glossy and wet
Frosty, chalky white
Yellow and translucent
Dark and stained
test.why: Etching removes a little surface mineral, so dried etched enamel looks frosty or chalky white.

whyNot.0: Glossy enamel hasn't been etched, or is still wet.
whyNot.2: Yellow translucency is more like dentine showing through, not etched enamel.
whyNot.3: Dark staining suggests decay or discolouration, not etching.

explain.body: Composite is placed with a plastic placement instrument in layers of about 2 mm, each cured with the light for the manufacturer's time. This gives full depth of cure and less shrinkage stress. The sticky oxygen-inhibited layer is normal.

test.q: Which instrument is designed to place and shape composite without sticking to it?
options: Amalgam carrier
Stainless cement spatula
Spoon excavator
Plastic instrument
test.why: A flat plastic (composite placement) instrument is designed to shape composite without dragging it out of the cavity.

whyNot.0: The amalgam carrier delivers amalgam, not composite.
whyNot.1: A cement spatula mixes cements on a slab or pad.

explain.body: The curing light gives out intense blue light that can harm the retina. Use the orange filter shield or orange glasses, never look at the tip, fit a barrier sleeve and check the light's output with a radiometer.

test.q: What is the main risk of looking at the curing light without protection?
options: Damage to the retina
Burns to the facial skin
Hearing damage
Ionising radiation dose
test.why: The intense blue light can damage the retina, so an orange filter shield or glasses must be used.

whyNot.1: The light can warm tissues, but the main risk from looking at it is to the eyes.
whyNot.2: Curing lights are silent and don't affect hearing.
whyNot.3: Curing lights produce visible light, not ionising radiation.
